unit-alg-t3-07.title: Topic 3 · 3-7 Transformations of Polynomial Functions
unit-alg-t3-07.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 3-7: Transformations of Polynomial Functions

summary.text: Lesson 3-7 applies the transformation rules to polynomial parent functions: g(x) = a · f(b(x − h)) + k, covering vertical and horizontal translations, stretches and compressions, and reflections.

why.text: These are the same transformation rules she has used on quadratics and absolute value, now on any polynomial — so the payoff is that one set of rules covers every function family she will meet.

objectives.text: Identify the parent function of a transformed polynomial
Describe translations, stretches, compressions and reflections from an equation
Track a point through a transformation
Predict the end behaviour of a transformed polynomial

parentNote.text:
The horizontal sign is the whole lesson: (x − 4) shifts RIGHT, not left, and it feels backwards to everyone. The fix that actually sticks is asking which x makes the bracket zero — that is where the parent’s origin ended up, and it is derivable rather than memorised, so it survives a stressful test. The same inversion governs horizontal stretches, where a factor greater than 1 SQUEEZES the graph.

One honest subtlety in a question here: for power functions a horizontal compression and a vertical stretch can produce the identical graph, since (2x)³ is also 8x³. That is a real feature of this family rather than an error, and the explanation says so.

nextUp.text: Track one point through each transformation — it settles every direction question.

cards.def:
**The simplest function of its family — x², x³, x⁴, x⁵ — before any transformation.**
• Every transformed polynomial in this lesson is one of these, moved, stretched or flipped.
• Even-degree parents open the same way at both ends; odd-degree parents run opposite ways.
cards.hint: Find the parent first. Everything else is a change made to it.

cards.def:
**g(x) = a · f(b(x − h)) + k.**
• a stretches vertically and flips it if negative; b stretches horizontally; h shifts left or right; k shifts up or down.
• The letters OUTSIDE the function (a and k) behave as you would expect; the ones INSIDE (b and h) do the opposite.
cards.hint: Outside is intuitive; inside is backwards.

cards.def:
**+ k moves the graph UP by k; − k moves it down.**
• It is added outside the function, so it does exactly what it looks like.
• f(x) = x³ + 5 is the cubic lifted five units.
cards.hint: Outside and last — the one transformation that never surprises anyone.

cards.def:
**f(x − h) moves the graph RIGHT by h, not left.**
• (x − 4)³ is the cubic shifted 4 units RIGHT; (x + 4)³ shifts it 4 LEFT.
• It feels backwards because the shift happens to the INPUT: to get the old output you now need a bigger x.
cards.eq: f(x − h) shifts right by h
cards.hint: The sign inside the bracket is the opposite of the direction of travel.

cards.def:
**a multiplies every output: |a| > 1 stretches it taller, 0 < |a| < 1 squashes it flatter.**
• 3x³ is three times as tall at every x; 0.2x³ is flattened.
• The x-intercepts never move under a vertical stretch — multiplying zero still gives zero.
cards.hint: Stretching vertically pins the zeros in place; only the heights change.

cards.def:
**A negative a flips the graph across the x-axis.**
• −f(x) sends every output to its opposite, so rises become falls.
• It reverses the end behaviour, and it leaves the x-intercepts exactly where they were.
cards.hint: A minus out front turns the picture upside down and moves no zero.

cards.def:
**f(bx) with |b| > 1 SQUEEZES the graph horizontally; 0 < |b| < 1 stretches it wider.**
• Backwards again, because b acts on the input: a bigger b means you reach the same output sooner.
• f(2x) is half as wide; f(0.5x) is twice as wide.
cards.hint: Big b, narrow graph. Inside the function, everything inverts.

cards.term: Even and odd degree under transformation
cards.def:
**A transformation never changes the degree, so it never changes whether the ends agree.**
• Shifting, stretching and flipping all preserve the degree.
• A reflection reverses which way the ends point, but an even-degree graph still has both ends together.
cards.hint: The ends can be flipped, but never un-matched.

cards.term: Reading a transformation off an equation
cards.def:
**Identify the parent, then take a, b, h and k one at a time.**
• g(x) = −2(x + 3)⁴ − 1: parent x⁴, reflected, stretched ×2, left 3, down 1.
• Note (x + 3) means LEFT 3, and the −1 outside means DOWN 1 — the two directions are read by different rules.
cards.hint: Name the parent out loud first. Then four small readings, not one big one.

cards.def:
**g(x) = (x − 2)³ + 1 is the parent cubic shifted 2 right and 1 up.**
• Its point of inflection sits at (2, 1), where the parent’s sits at the origin.
• The shape is completely unchanged — only its position moved.
cards.hint: Translations move the graph and never reshape it.

cards.def:
**h(x) = −0.5x⁴ is the quartic reflected across the x-axis and squashed to half height.**
• The parent x⁴ has both ends up; the minus sends both ends down.
• The 0.5 flattens it but moves nothing — the only zero, at the origin, stays put.
cards.hint: Sign flips it, size flattens it, and neither moves a zero.

questions.q: How does the graph of g(x) = x³ + 7 compare with f(x) = x³?
questions.hint: The 7 is added outside the function.
steps: The change is added AFTER cubing, so it acts on the output.
Adding to the output raises every point.
So the graph moves up.
Shifted 7 units up.

ex.main: **Shifted 7 units up.** Changes outside the function do what they look like they do. A horizontal shift would need the 7 inside the cube, as (x + 7)³ — and that one moves LEFT, not right.
ex.tip: Outside the function: vertical, and intuitive.

questions.q: How does the graph of g(x) = (x − 6)⁴ compare with f(x) = x⁴?
questions.hint: A change inside the function does the opposite of what it looks like.
steps: The 6 is subtracted from x, so it is INSIDE the function.
Inside changes act horizontally and run backwards.
Subtracting moves the graph in the POSITIVE direction.
So it shifts 6 units right.

ex.main: **Shifted 6 units right.** Minus means right. The reason is that the shift acts on the INPUT: to get the output the parent gave at 0, you now have to feed in x = 6. That "you need a bigger x" reasoning is what makes the direction stick.
ex.tip: When in doubt, ask what x makes the bracket zero. That x is where the parent’s origin ended up.

questions.q: What does the negative sign do in g(x) = −x⁵?
opts: Reflects the graph across the y-axis
Reflects the graph across the x-axis
questions.hint: A minus in front multiplies every output by −1.
steps: The minus multiplies the whole function, so it acts on outputs.
Every output becomes its opposite.
Positive values go below the axis and negative values go above.
That is a reflection across the x-axis.

ex.main: **Reflects across the x-axis.** A reflection across the y-AXIS would need the minus inside, as (−x)⁵ — acting on the input rather than the output. For an odd function like x⁵ those two happen to produce the same picture, but they are different operations and on most functions they differ.
ex.tip: Minus outside flips vertically; minus inside flips horizontally.

questions.q: In g(x) = 4x³, what does the 4 do?
opts: Compresses the graph vertically by a factor of 4
Stretches the graph vertically by a factor of 4
questions.hint: It multiplies the output, and it is bigger than 1.
steps: The 4 multiplies the whole function, so it acts on outputs.
Multiplying outputs by a number bigger than 1 makes them further from the axis.
So the graph is stretched vertically.
It is a vertical stretch by a factor of 4.

ex.main: **Stretches vertically by a factor of 4.** A factor greater than 1 stretches; a factor between 0 and 1 would compress. Note the zero at the origin does not move — 4 × 0 is still 0, which is why vertical stretching never relocates an x-intercept.
ex.tip: Vertical stretches change heights and leave every zero exactly where it is.

questions.q: Which parent function does g(x) = −3(x + 1)⁴ − 2 come from?
questions.hint: The parent is the simplest function of the family — no coefficients, no shifts.
steps: The power on the bracket is 4.
So the family is the quartics.
The parent of that family is the simplest one: x⁴.
The −3, the +1 and the −2 are all transformations applied to it.

ex.main: **x⁴.** The parent never carries any of the transformations — −x⁴ already has the reflection built in, so it is a transformed function rather than a parent. Identifying the bare power first is what makes the rest of the reading straightforward.
ex.tip: Strip everything away until only the power is left. That is the parent.

questions.q: Describe every transformation in g(x) = −2(x − 5)³ + 4 from the parent x³.
questions.hint: Take a, h and k one at a time, and remember which of them run backwards.
steps: a = −2: the minus reflects across the x-axis and the 2 stretches vertically.
The bracket is (x − 5), which shifts RIGHT 5 — inside changes run opposite to their sign.
The + 4 is outside, so it shifts UP 4.
Reflected, stretched by 2, right 5, up 4.

ex.main: **Reflected, stretched by 2, right 5, up 4.** Three readings, three different rules: the sign of a reflects, its size stretches (2 > 1, so stretch not compress), and the bracket’s minus means right while the outside plus means up. Reading them one at a time is what stops them blurring together.
ex.tip: Say each one out loud as you take it. Four quick decisions beat one complicated one.

questions.q: The point (2, 8) is on f(x) = x³. Where is the corresponding point on g(x) = f(x − 3) + 5?
questions.hint: Apply the horizontal shift to the x-coordinate and the vertical one to the y.
steps: f(x − 3) shifts the graph 3 units right, so x goes from 2 to 5.
The + 5 shifts it 5 units up, so y goes from 8 to 13.
Both coordinates move, each by its own transformation.
The point lands at (5, 13).

ex.main: **(5, 13).** Tracking one point is the fastest way to check a transformation you are unsure of: the minus inside really does move it in the POSITIVE x direction. Getting (−1, 13) means applying the horizontal shift the wrong way — the exact error the sign trap produces.
ex.tip: Follow a single known point through. It settles every direction question without a graph.

questions.q: Which transformation does NOT move any x-intercept of a polynomial?
questions.hint: Ask which change leaves outputs of zero still equal to zero.
steps: A vertical stretch multiplies every output by a constant.
Any output that was 0 becomes a · 0 = 0, so it stays a zero.
A vertical translation shifts zeros off the axis entirely.
Both horizontal changes move the x-values themselves. So only the vertical stretch leaves them put.

ex.main: **A vertical stretch.** Multiplying by a non-zero constant cannot create or destroy a zero, so the x-intercepts are exactly where they were — only the heights between them changed. Every other transformation here moves them: vertically by lifting the graph off the axis, horizontally by relocating the x-values.
ex.tip: A reflection is also a vertical multiplication, so it leaves the zeros alone too.

questions.q: How does g(x) = (2x)³ compare with f(x) = x³?
opts: Horizontally compressed by a factor of 2
Horizontally stretched by a factor of 2
Vertically stretched by a factor of 2
questions.hint: The 2 is inside the function, so it acts horizontally — and backwards.
steps: The 2 multiplies x before the cubing, so it is an inside change.
Inside changes act horizontally and run opposite to expectation.
A factor greater than 1 therefore SQUEEZES rather than stretches.
So it is horizontally compressed by a factor of 2.

ex.main: **Horizontally compressed by 2.** Bigger b means a narrower graph, because you reach any given output at half the x you used to. Note that (2x)³ also equals 8x³ — so this one can honestly be described as a vertical stretch by 8 as well, which is a genuine quirk of power functions rather than a contradiction.
ex.tip: For power functions, a horizontal squeeze and a vertical stretch can be the same graph.

questions.q: A student says (x + 3)² shifts the parabola 3 units right because of the plus. What is the clearest way to show them otherwise?
opts: Point out that a plus inside always means a shift left
Ask which x makes the bracket zero — it is −3, so it moved left
Expand it to x² + 6x + 9 and read off the middle term
Note that the parabola opens upward whichever sign is used
questions.hint: Look for the argument that shows WHY, not just a rule to memorise.
steps: The parent x² has its vertex where its input is 0.
For (x + 3)², the input to the squaring is (x + 3).
That is zero when x = −3.
So the vertex now sits at x = −3 — three units LEFT.

ex.main: **Ask which x makes the bracket zero.** That single question settles the direction from first principles every time, without memorising a rule that feels backwards. "A plus always means left" is correct but is just another rule to take on trust, and expanding it hides the structure completely.
ex.tip: Set the inside to zero. Wherever that lands is where the parent’s origin ended up.

questions.q: g(x) = −(x − 1)⁴ + 3. What is its end behaviour and where is its maximum?
questions.hint: The degree decides whether the ends agree; the reflection decides which way; the shifts place the peak.
steps: The degree is 4, which is even, so both ends agree.
The leading coefficient is negative (the reflection), so both ends go DOWN.
The parent x⁴ has its minimum at the origin; reflecting turns that into a maximum.
The shifts move it right 1 and up 3, so the maximum is at (1, 3).

ex.main: **Both ends down; maximum at (1, 3).** Three independent readings that have to agree: even degree pairs the ends, the minus sends them down, and the reflection converts the parent’s lowest point into a highest one. Since both ends fall, that peak really is the highest point overall.
ex.tip: A reflected even-degree polynomial always has a genuine maximum. Both ends falling guarantees it.

questions.q: Why does a transformation never change whether a polynomial’s two ends point the same way?
opts: Because end behaviour is not affected by transformations at all
Because transformations only move graphs, never reshape them
Because the leading coefficient never changes
Because no transformation changes the degree, and the degree’s parity decides it
questions.hint: Two things set the end behaviour. Ask which of them a transformation can touch.
steps: Whether the ends agree depends only on whether the degree is even or odd.
Shifting, stretching and reflecting all leave the degree exactly as it was.
So the parity is untouched, and the ends keep agreeing or keep disagreeing.
A reflection can swap which way they point, but never un-pair them.

ex.main: **Because no transformation changes the degree.** The leading coefficient certainly CAN change — a reflection negates it, which reverses the ends’ direction — so end behaviour is affected; what cannot change is whether the two ends match, because that is decided by parity alone.
ex.tip: Direction can flip. Agreement cannot. The two halves of end behaviour are set by different things.

questions.q: Put these transformations of f(x) = x⁴ in order from NARROWEST to WIDEST graph.
questions.hint: A larger vertical stretch makes the graph rise faster, which reads as narrower.
steps: A bigger multiplier makes every output larger, so the graph climbs more steeply.
Climbing steeply means it reaches a given height sooner — it looks narrower.
So the order runs from the largest coefficient to the smallest.
5, then 2, then 0.5, then 0.1.

ex.main: **5, 2, 0.5, then 0.1.** A bigger vertical stretch reads as a narrower graph, because the curve reaches any given height at a smaller x. Coefficients between 0 and 1 flatten it out, which reads as wider — and none of them moves the zero at the origin.
ex.tip: Narrow and wide are descriptions of steepness here, not of anything horizontal actually changing.

questions.q: In g(x) = ⅓x³, what does the ⅓ do to the graph of f(x) = x³?
opts: Compresses it vertically, so it climbs more slowly
Stretches it vertically, so it climbs more quickly
Shifts the whole graph down by one third of a unit
Reflects the whole graph across the x-axis
questions.hint: Every output is cut to a third of what it was. Picture what that does to the height.
steps: A number multiplying the whole function acts on the OUTPUT.
Each y-value becomes a third of its old size.
Points move toward the x-axis rather than away from it.
That is a vertical compression, and the graph climbs more slowly.

ex.main: **A vertical compression — it climbs more slowly.** A multiplier bigger than 1 stretches; a multiplier between 0 and 1 compresses. The word "compression" describes the SHAPE and not a direction of movement: nothing slides down the page, every point simply lands closer to the axis than it used to.
ex.tip: Bigger than 1 stretches, between 0 and 1 squashes. The sign is a separate question.

questions.q: What does the minus sign INSIDE the parentheses do in g(x) = (−x)³?
opts: Reflects the graph across the x-axis
Reflects the graph across the y-axis
Shifts the graph to the left
questions.hint: Inside the parentheses is always about the input, which is the horizontal direction.
steps: A change inside the parentheses acts on the INPUT, so it is horizontal.
Negating the input swaps what happens at x with what happens at −x.
Left and right trade places, which is a reflection across the y-axis.
A minus OUTSIDE would instead flip up and down, across the x-axis.

ex.main: **A reflection across the y-axis.** Inside acts on the input and is horizontal; outside acts on the output and is vertical. These two are the pair most often swapped, and for an odd power they happen to draw the same picture — (−x)³ equals −x³ — which is exactly why the reasoning matters more than the drawing. For an even power they are genuinely different.
ex.tip: Inside → input → horizontal. Outside → output → vertical.

questions.q: Write the function for y = x³ reflected across the x-axis, moved 4 units left, then moved 1 unit up.
questions.hint: The horizontal move is the one where the written sign is the opposite of the movement.
steps: Reflecting across the x-axis puts a minus on the whole function: −x³.
Moving 4 LEFT means replacing x with x + 4, because inside signs work backwards.
Moving 1 UP adds 1 on the outside, where the sign is straightforward.
Putting them together: g(x) = −(x + 4)³ + 1.

ex.main: **g(x) = −(x + 4)³ + 1.** Only the horizontal move reverses: left is written as a plus, right as a minus, because it is the input being adjusted before the function ever runs. The vertical pieces read exactly as they look, so up really is + 1.
ex.tip: Left is +, right is −, and only inside the parentheses. Vertical shifts say what they mean.

questions.q: g(x) = 5(x − 2)⁴. Where is its minimum, and what is the minimum value there?
opts: At x = 0, and the minimum value is 0
At x = −2, and the minimum value is 0
At x = 2, and the minimum value is 5
At x = 2, and the minimum value is 0
questions.hint: A fourth power is never negative, so ask where it manages to be zero.
steps: (x − 2)⁴ is never negative, and it is zero exactly when x = 2.
Multiplying by 5 does not change WHERE the zero is.
5 × 0 is still 0, so the minimum value stays 0.
The minimum is 0, at x = 2.

ex.main: **At x = 2, with value 0.** A vertical stretch pulls the graph away from the x-axis everywhere except on the axis itself, where five times nothing is still nothing — so the lowest point does not move at all. Only a vertical SHIFT would change the minimum value, and there is not one here.
ex.tip: A stretch moves everything except the points already sitting on the axis.

questions.q: The point (1, 5) lies on f. Which point must lie on g(x) = f(x + 2) − 6?
questions.hint: Ask what input to g makes the inside of f equal 1.
steps: g reads f at x + 2, so set x + 2 = 1 to reach the known point.
That gives x = −1, so the new point sits at −1 on the x-axis.
At that input f returns 5, and g then subtracts 6.
5 − 6 = −1, so the point is (−1, −1).

ex.main: **(−1, −1).** The + 2 inside moves the graph LEFT, so the x-coordinate goes down rather than up — (3, −1) is what you get by adding 2 in the direction the plus suggests. The − 6 outside is straightforward and simply lowers the height by 6.
ex.tip: Solve inside = old x. Then do the outside arithmetic to the y-value.

questions.q: Does order matter? Route A stretches f(x) = x³ vertically by 3 and then shifts up 2. Route B shifts up 2 and then stretches by 3.
opts: No — both routes end at 3x³ + 2, so the order makes no difference here
Yes — A gives 3x³ + 2, B gives 3x³ + 6; the stretch multiplies the shift
No — both routes end at 3x³ + 6, so the order makes no difference here
Yes — A gives 3x³ + 6 and B gives 3x³ + 2, the other way round
questions.hint: Write each route out as an expression rather than picturing it.
steps: Route A: stretch first gives 3x³, then adding 2 gives 3x³ + 2.
Route B: shift first gives x³ + 2, then stretching gives 3(x³ + 2).
Expanding that second one gives 3x³ + 6.
The two results differ, so the order does matter.

ex.main: **Yes — A gives 3x³ + 2 and B gives 3x³ + 6.** Stretching after a shift multiplies the shift as well, which is why a written form like a(x − h)ⁿ + k always means stretch first and shift second. Reading a function left to right is not the order the transformations happen in.
ex.tip: A stretch applied later multiplies whatever was already added.

questions.q: g(x) = (x − 4)⁵ + 1. How many real zeros does it have, and where?
opts: None — a fifth power can never come out negative
Five, at x = 3 — the exponent counts how many zeros there are
One, at x = 3 — an odd power hits each value exactly once
One, at x = 5 — subtract the 1 from the 4 inside the parentheses
questions.hint: Set it to zero and undo the pieces one at a time. Odd roots of negatives are allowed.
steps: Setting g(x) = 0 gives (x − 4)⁵ = −1.
An odd power can be negative, and the only real fifth root of −1 is −1.
So x − 4 = −1, which gives x = 3.
An odd power takes each value exactly once, so x = 3 is the only real zero.

ex.main: **One real zero, at x = 3.** An odd power is one-to-one, so the equation has exactly one real solution no matter what is on the right — unlike an even power, where (x − 4)⁴ = 1 would give two. The exponent counts roots with multiplicity over the complex numbers, not distinct real crossings, so five is the wrong reading of it.
ex.tip: Odd power → one real solution every time. Even power → two, or none.
